title: Ten extra or ten percent extra
hook: Ten extra or 10% extra: which order is bigger depends on the job size.

knows: that a model can declare hypothetical quantities
doesNotKnow: Distinguish a proportional allowance from a fixed spare count.

misconception: Ten percent extra always means ten extra pieces.
objective: Distinguish a proportional allowance from a fixed spare count.

claims.text: Compare an order with 10% extra, rounded up, against an order with ten extra tiles. Scaled model; quantity-only model; no installation advice.
claims.source: Declared hypothetical inputs and limits in resource-specs.json. No actual product, price, tariff, shelf-life, treatment or physical appliance specification is asserted. FC LH-2 (2026-10-14, fresh fact-checker instance, W-369): verified: matches the rendered question and the assumptions line ("Full scale:132tiles; quantity-only model; no installation advice."; "Scaled model" there is the full-scale prefix).

claims.text: The stage's two results are computed by the printed expressions. At Required=40tiles, A=44tiles and B=50tiles. Geometry follows the declared dimension relationships. Other pictures use a fixed full scale across the slider range; continuous fills and arcs show relative amounts rather than literal object counts.
claims.source: src/lib/lifehacks/resource-specs.json contains this lesson's numeric AST; src/lib/lifehacks/resource-model.ts evaluates it. A=["ceil",["*","x",1.1]]; B=["+","x",10]; x denotes Required. At x=40, A=44, B=50. Before ceil, resource-model.ts snaps a product within 1e-9 of an integer (snapToInteger), so x=100 gives A=ceil(110)=110, not 111 (W-357). On the slider (20 to 120, step 5) A=B at x=95 (ceil(104.5)=105) and x=100 (110); A<B below 95 and A>B from 105. Values are fictional/ideal assumptions, not measurements. Display rounds to at most three decimals. Diagram scale: resourceGraphicScale in resource-model.ts takes the maximum modeled magnitude across both formulas and the declared slider range. For non-geometry figures, full-scale values are displayed; the scale stays fixed when the slider changes. Energy axis endpoints use resourceAxisEnd, including B=5×A hours in lh-watts-hours-trade; cylinder rx and ry both scale with radius in resourceCylinderDimensions. FC LH-2 (2026-10-14, fresh fact-checker instance, W-369): verified: stage prints ceil((40×1.1)) = 44tiles and (40+10) = 50tiles; fills are proportional; Full scale 132 = resourceGraphicScale = A at 120, fixed across x=40,95,100,105 screenshots.

claims.text: A fixed extra count stays ten. A percentage extra grows with the requirement. At forty, 10% is four; at one hundred, 10% is ten. Rounding up also ties them at 95; above 100 the percentage order is larger.
claims.source: src/lib/lifehacks/resource-specs.json contains this lesson's numeric AST; src/lib/lifehacks/resource-model.ts evaluates it. A=["ceil",["*","x",1.1]]; B=["+","x",10]; x denotes Required. At x=40, A=44, B=50. Before ceil, resource-model.ts snaps a product within 1e-9 of an integer (snapToInteger), so x=100 gives A=ceil(110)=110, not 111 (W-357). On the slider (20 to 120, step 5) A=B at x=95 (ceil(104.5)=105) and x=100 (110); A<B below 95 and A>B from 105. Values are fictional/ideal assumptions, not measurements. Display rounds to at most three decimals. The principle follows from those expressions and stated scenario limits. FC LH-2 (2026-10-14, fresh fact-checker instance, W-369): verified with exact integer arithmetic, not the model: A = ceil(11x/10) = floor((11x+9)/10); A=B exactly for integers 91..100, i.e. 95 and 100 on the step-5 slider; A<B at 20..90, A>B at 105..120; resource-model.ts (snapToInteger) matches exact values at all 21 slider points, and the stage shows 105/105, 110/110, 116/115. "Rounding up also ties them at 95" is true and slider-scoped.

claims.text: From what required count is 10% extra (rounded up) at least as large as ten extra? Correct: 91. 10% grows with the requirement; the two orders are equal for requirements from 91 to 100 (95 and 100 on the slider), and below that ten extra is larger.

Wording came verbatim from an FC LH-1 example; this is the fresh instance under the W-280 ruling (see the fact-check record for the reading-order disclosure).

claims.text: Ten extra or 10% extra: which order is bigger depends on the job size.
claims.source: Hook (meta.json hook; resource-specs.json "lh-percentage-overage".hook), reworded under W-384 on 2026-10-14 by demo-builder after FC LH-2 disputed the old hook "A fixed spare count and a percentage spare count diverge as a job grows." (the spare counts converge, then cross, on the stage). Derivation: A=ceil(1.1x) (10% extra, rounded up) and B=x+10 (ten extra); on the slider (20 to 120, step 5) B>A below 95, A=B at 95 and 100, and A>B from 105 (src/lib/lifehacks/resource-model.ts with snapToInteger; same values as c3). So which order is bigger depends on the required count. The hook names no crossover value.

recall.question: From what required count is 10% extra (rounded up) at least as large as ten extra?
recall.why: 10% grows with the requirement; the two orders are equal for requirements from 91 to 100 (95 and 100 on the slider), and below that ten extra is larger.
